extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of moral and political philosophy; philosophers interested in ethics, metaphysics, and jurisprudence
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpts from a philosophical treatise addressing the metaphysics of the will, foundations of ethics, and principles of law and statecraft, with concrete prescriptions for property, punishment, and political institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of moral guilt (operari sequitur esse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral guilt ultimately stems from the will or the being (operari sequitur esse); when a being has another origin, guilt falls back upon that origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a person's deeds flow necessarily from his essential will or origin, then moral responsibility traces to that underlying will/essence. This principle grounds several later claims about original sin, determinism of character, and responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right exists independently of the State
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who deny a right apart from the State confuse the means for enforcing right with the right itself; the right exists independently even though the State provides its protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The State secures and enforces rights but does not create their moral existence; force can suppress rights but never abolish their moral reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aims of the State — (1) Outward protection (law of nations)
rubrics_metrics.description: First aim: outward protection against lifeless nature, wild beasts, other men and other nations; nations profess a defensive posture and thereby recognise 'the law of nations'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sphere is the practical domain of natural law between nations where positive law cannot fully operate; public opinion serves as the tribunal enforcing honour among nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aims of the State — (2) Internal protection (security of private right)
rubrics_metrics.description: Second aim: protection of members of the State against each other, securing private rights by maintaining honest conditions so that concentrated forces of all protect each individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The State's internal role is to create social conditions that effectively secure individual rights and appearance of general honesty/justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aims of the State — (3) Protection against the protector (separation of powers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Third aim: protection against those entrusted with protection — guarantee of public right; achieved by dividing legislator, judicature, and executive so each is independent of the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the safeguard of liberty: separate powers to prevent abuse by protectors; underlies advocacy for institutional checks and balances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property arises from labour
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of property arises only through the expenditure of labour upon things; property is 'embodied work'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is supported by historical and practical argumentation (e.g., cultivated fields, constructed habitations belong morally to those who laboured). It is used to rebut extreme claims that Europeans had no right to appropriate certain lands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral recognition distinguishes theft from poaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Though law may punish poaching as severely as theft, civil honour is lost by theft but not by poaching; game is not an object of morally valid possession because labour has not been bestowed on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morally valid possession requires labour; absence of labour makes certain legal claims merely positive rather than morally recognised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment should target the deed to deter, not to punish the man
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle: it is not the man but the deed that should be punished, so that the law's deterrent power is preserved; punishment aims at deterring recurrence rather than retribution of the person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with Kantian retribution (jus talionis) and penitentiary goals of reform. The author criticises attempts to use a single means to achieve opposing ends (punishment as both evil and education).

rubrics_metrics.name: Penitentiary reform is problematic; reformation is doubtful
rubrics_metrics.description: Because inborn character is unalterable, moral reformation is not really possible; punishment should aim at deterrence through fear, while correction of knowledge and awakening desire to work may have some effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given a presumed fixed character, prisons cannot reliably reform moral character; educational measures may help practical outcomes but cannot alter essential moral character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design punishments so apparent severity exceeds actual severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, the apparent severity of punishment ought to exceed the actual; solitary confinement fails because its great severity has no witnesses and is therefore not anticipated and does not deter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deterrence depends on the expectation of punishment. If a punishment's worst effects are hidden (as with solitary confinement), it will not deter those tempted by crime; visible threats are more effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality of punishment (Beccaria's insight, but a different rationale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Punishment ought to bear a proper proportion to the crime — not because it expiates but because the pledge must be proportionate to the value of what it secures; e.g., life may justify capital punishment for protection of life, but not to preserve ure-oxen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Severity should match the importance of the interest protected (life vs property). This grounds a utilitarian/guardianship rationale for proportional sanctions rather than retributive justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure punishment by magnitude of injury and strength of motives
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining punishment, consider (a) magnitude of the injury to be guarded against, (b) the strength of the motives that impel to the forbidden action, (c) difficulty of convicting the criminal—the stronger the temptation and the harder the conviction, the stronger the counter-motive (punishment) must be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The criminal code should act as a register of counter-motives that decisively outweigh motives for crime. This presumes the will is determined by motives and uses that to calibrate deterrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of inclination, passion, and emotion (and their moral relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclination: strong susceptibility of the will for certain motives. Passion: an inclination so strong that motives exciting it overpower the will and render it passive. Emotion: a passing irresistible excitement that momentarily abolishes intellectual freedom by excluding counter-motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions explain degrees of diminished intellectual freedom and ground moral responsibility and the possibility of repentance: emotion is like delirium to passion's madness; passions often approximate but do not always reach full definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral repentance arises from post-act apprehension of counter-motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Repentance occurs when, after the act, counter-motives present themselves as consequences already experienced, making the agent aware that he acted without full intellectual freedom; the originally motivating inclination or emotion is neutralised by reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include crimes driven by revenge, jealousy, avarice, or marriages concluded in passionate love. Repentance indicates that the motives which led to the act failed to allow full deliberation; it highlights relative weakness of intellect in the face of the will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness (σωφροσυνη) as the alignment of intellect and will
rubrics_metrics.description: True reasonableness consists in the intellect never being overpowered by the will to the extent that it cannot present motives distinctly and fully; it requires a suitable relation between the will and a relatively strong intellect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This character trait can arise from either moderation of the will or strength of intellect; virtue is not exclusive to high intellect because the necessary metaphysical insight may be simple and accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchy as institutional neutralisation of egoism; hereditary rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of monarchy lies in placing one person so high (power, wealth, inviolability) that personal desires are neutralised, enabling supposedly disinterested justice; consequently monarchy should be hereditary, not elective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hereditary monarchy is argued to prevent equality that breeds private ambition in the sovereign and to bind the monarch to concern for successors (family), aligning his interest with the public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathy as the empirical basis of justice and benevolence
rubrics_metrics.description: Sympathy (the empirical appearance of the metaphysical identity of the will) is the basis of justice and caritas (benevolence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This metaphysical identity yields sympathy which underpins moral behavior; seeing others as metaphysical continuations of oneself grounds altruism and justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three principal phenomena of the metaphysical identity of the will (sympathies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three principal phenomena dependent on the metaphysical identity of the will: (1) sympathy proper (basis of justice and benevolence), (2) sexual love (amor) which serves the life of the species, (3) magic (including animal magnetism and sympathetic cures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are empirical manifestations of a deeper metaphysical unity and explain different forms of interpersonal connection — moral, biological, and (allegedly) occult/therapeutic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theodicy and the denial of pantheism given suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Pantheism (or regarding the world as theophany) collapses ethics since if all is divine nothing is censorable; the reality of suffering, evil, and misery refutes pantheism and demands an ethical ordering not derivable from a purely physical theophany.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an evaluative standard for philosophical systems: they must account for moral difference and suffering; systems that render good/evil merely conventional fail to sustain ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christian myth: works do not justify; original sin rooted in existence/will
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian doctrine (and similar doctrines in Brahmanism/Buddhism) holds that works cannot justify because humans are essentially sinners through their very existence/will; salvation requires a complete transformation (new birth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The argument ties theological teaching to metaphysical claim operari sequitur esse — since being determines acting, a corrupted being necessitates sinful action and thus requires radical change rather than mere moral effort.
